publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Associate Member): I am afraid I have given an erroneous impression of my views on “hunting.” While admitting that rotaries are particularly sensitive to this trouble, I do not think they are the cause of it. I maintain the cause is in the prime mover. Bearing in mind the frequency of the impulses, and compare that with the frequency of the dynamic irregularities in angular velocity of most steam engines, there is a great difference. (I refer to the variation in speed due to the inertia of the reciprocating parts, and the difference in pressure of the steam due to expansion and total pressure tangentially to the flywheel, due to angular position of the connecting rod). “Hunting” occurs with slow, medium and high speed reciprocating engines and turbines. Consequently it appears that this trouble is largely due to irregularity in the admission of steam to the prime movers. My practical experience bears out this theory, having stopped “hunting” many times by a slight adjustment of the governor or even by just steadying the governor rod by hand. The provision of a good dash pot on the governor rods is of great value in this respect. Dampers are most necessary when dealing with a load that consists almost entirely of synchronous machines. Where there is less than 50 per cent. of induction motors on the system, the trifling extra expense of dampers is well worth the freedom obtained from “hunting.”

articleTitle: Selection and types of induction motors

abstract: It is assumed that the choice of an induction motor is governed by the following considerations: — (1) Nature of the current supply, pressure and frequency. (2) Nature of the work and conditions under which the motor operates. These conditions include the starting torque required, that is to say, whether the motor is to start light or fully loaded — speed, continuous or intermittent loads, direct coupled, geared or arranged for a belt or rope drive. (3) Economic conditions, initial capital outlay, cost of installation and probable operating and maintenance costs.

abstract: (Member): I agree with the author that all apparatus should be either well and properly earthed, or well and properly insulated. The latter is difficult to attain and maintain. The former is comparatively easy, both to attain and maintain, but it is very necessary that “earthing” shall not be done promiscuously. It is wortb going to the expense of making some special provision that your “earth” may be uniform, because thereby human life may sometimes be saved. Both in this country and elsewhere deaths have been caused due to the lack of this provision. An “earth” should be chosen which will run fairly uniformly over the whole district in which the supply is to be distributed.

abstract: (Member): The authors of this paper have brought forward a most interesting subject, and I think we must all agree that in doing so they have displayed much ingenuity and enterprise. In bringing before this Institute an unproved attempt to solve this very difficult problem, they court criticism, and will, I am sure, be the first to welcome comments, whether favourable or adverse, from the members. As our President has repeatedly pointed out, the value and efficiency of the Institute depends very largely upon a full and careful discussion of the papers read, and I should like to point out that it is particularly necessary in the case of a paper, such as that now under discussion, that members should express their views, so that the matter may be left clear. An Institute like ours should stand for the consensus of opinion of local electrical engineers, and it is, therefore, up to us to criticise the views held by the authors of this paper openly and freely.

abstract: (Member): I regret that pressure of work has prevented me contributing as I should have liked to the discussion on Mr. Perrow's valuable and interesting paper, but there is one point which I feel it my duty to comment on, and that is the use of the Faradic coil to assist artificial respiration. That this method is of the greatest value there can be no doubt, and I have provided for use on the mine where I am employed two such coils, but these coils are kept locked up and reserved for use by a doctor only, for the following reason: About a quarter of an inch from the right phrenic nerve in the neck, where the rheophore has to be applied, lies the vagus nerve, and the result of Faradisation of this nerve would be to inhibit the heart's action, and I think you will agree with me that it would be too great a risk to entrust to ourselves or other non-medical men the selection of the correct spot to apply the rheophore, where a mistake of one-quarter of an inch would be fatal. I have also provided with these coils special rheophores, having a point like a ½-inch cold chisel, covered with chamois leather, in order that the doctor may easily make contact on the exact spot.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Member): I have only one point to enlarge upon on this paper, viz., the protective devices for motors. The author describes overload and no-volt releases. The latter, to my mind, are most essential, and I do not think they can be too strongly insisted upon. So far as my experience has gone, it appears to me that hitherto their utility has not been appreciated on the Rand, and yet I suppose their absence has been the cause of the loss of quite a lot of valuable time, when temporary breakdowns have occurred. When one considers that a mine making a profit of, say, only £1,000 per month is losing more than £1 profit each hour the plant is stopped, it can very readily be seen that the time saved by the use of no-volt releases may very easily repay the cost of their purchase in a very short time. On the other hand, their absence may quite easily cause serious damage, and further loss to valuable motors. Hence their general adoption should very strongly be urged.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Electric Power in Colleries. — A paper by Mr. F. Anslow, entitled, “Some Considerations affecting the installation of Power at Collieries,” was among those discussed at the meeting at Dunfermline of the Mining Institute of Scotland, on June 17th. Mr. Anslow, in dealing with existing steam plants at collieries, said that these were often destitute of condensing plant, partly on account of difficulties in running winding engines condensing, but he showed that in most cases, except where increased power is required, the cost of adding condensers to improve the economy was not justified. Where extensions are required, however condensing plant and exhaust, or mixed turbines driving electrical generators, will render considerable extra power available without extra steam being required from the boilers. Details were given of a case where an extra 500 KW. was thus made available. Even where a large proportion of steam plant is already condensing, considerable extra power can be obtained by the installation of mixed pressure turbo plant, and particulars were given of an example to illustrate this.

abstract: The Action of the X-Ray in Large and Small Doses. — Since the discovery of the X-rays and their application to therapeutics, many and various results have been obtained from their use, results often quite contradictory in character, the explanations of which have at times been distinctly puzzling. It has been difficult in many instances to explain why in one case the use of the rays would cause degeneration and at others regeneration of similar tissues; why, for example, in one patient superflous hair would be removed and in another the use of the rays on a smooth skin would result in a profuse hirsute adornment. In recent years, however means have been devised of regulating the dose of the X-rays and of estimating in units the amount of radiation being administered in each case. This has made the study of the action more accurate and has enabled the illumination of several obscure points. In the Berliner klinische Wochenschrift for May 23, 1910, H. E. Schmidt reports a small series of experiments into the effect of various doses of the X-ray upon cell growth. Having soaked a number of beans in water for six hours he treated the different beans with different doses of rays, and then planted them. His results were quite uniform and demonstrated two points of interest. Whereas those beans which were treated with large doses of the rays were partially or completely inhibited in their growth, as compared to untreated control beans, those which received very small doses were distinctly stimulated; not only were the plants larger and more vigorous, but the flowers were larger and the resulting crop of beans better. From these findings Schmidt suggests that the same principle may apply to animal cells, and experiments which he carried out on an ulcer on the arm suggested that this is the case. If this be so, it is evident that in treating conditions in which healing is desired, as a sluggish ulcer, very small doses of the X-ray should be used, whereas in cases of malignant growth, where tissue destruction is required, large doses are needed, and small doses instead of destraying the neoplasm may do harm rather than good by stimulating it to renewed activity. — Electrical Review and Western Electrician, July 30. 1910, p. 234.

Acceleration curves are useful, especially when there are numerous short trips, because the higher the acceleration, the more economical the run.
